title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
summary: Job answers Bildad by describing how God has walled him in, stripped his honor, and besieged him like an army, while his brothers, friends, servants, and even his wife have turned from him. He begs his friends for pity and wishes his words could be carved in rock forever. Then he makes the book's most famous declaration: his Redeemer lives, will stand upon the earth at the last, and Job himself will see God with his own eyes.
story: Bildad has just painted the wicked man's end in images drawn from Job's own losses: fire, dead children, disease, a forgotten name (chapter 18). Job's answer is the emotional summit of the dialogue. First he descends further than before, describing not only God's attack but the total abandonment of every human relationship he has. Then, from that lowest place, he rises higher than at any point in the book. The line of hope that began with his lament that there was no mediator (9:33) and grew into his confidence in a witness in heaven (16:19) and his plea for a guarantor (17:3) reaches its peak here. After this, the second round continues with Zophar (chapter 20), but nothing in the friends' speeches matches the height of verses 25-27.
historical:
Job's wish in verses 23-24 reflects the ways the ancient world preserved important words. Scrolls were written on papyrus or leather. Lasting records were cut into stone: kings carved inscriptions into cliff faces and monuments, such as the great rock inscription of the Persian king Darius I at Behistun, from around 520 BC, so that their deeds would outlast them. Writing with an iron stylus on lead may mean letters incised in lead, or letters cut in rock and filled with lead to make them stand out; interpreters are unsure which is meant. Job wants his testimony preserved in the most permanent form possible, so that even after his death his innocence could be read.

The siege image in verse 12 also belongs to ancient warfare. Armies built earthen ramps up to the walls of a city to bring battering rams against them, a method used by Assyrian and Babylonian forces. Job feels that God has brought an entire army, ramp and camp, against a single tent.
cultural:
The key word of verse 25, Redeemer (go'el), comes from Israel's family law. A go'el was the nearest male relative, responsible for protecting a family member in trouble. He bought back land a poor relative had been forced to sell (Leviticus 25:25), redeemed a relative sold into slavery (Leviticus 25:47-49), avenged the blood of a murdered kinsman (Numbers 35:19), and could marry a childless widow to continue the family name, as Boaz did for Ruth (Ruth 3:9-13; 4:1-10). The same word is used of God as Israel's Redeemer, especially in Isaiah (Isaiah 41:14; 43:14). Job has just said his brothers and kinsmen have abandoned him (verses 13-14). With no human go'el left, he declares that he has one who lives.

The list of abandonments in verses 13-19 reflects how much identity depended on the household. Brothers, relatives, guests, servants, a wife, children in the street, and close friends formed the whole web of a man's life. Losing their respect meant losing his place in the world.
literary: The chapter builds carefully to its climax. Verses 2-6 rebuke the friends and insist that God, not Job, has done wrong in this case. Verses 7-12 describe God's attack in images of a blocked road, a stripped crown, an uprooted tree, and a besieging army. Verses 13-20 list the loss of every human relationship, ending with the proverbial phrase “I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.” Verses 21-22 plead for pity. Verses 23-24 wish for a permanent record. Then verses 25-27 break through with the declaration of faith, three times insisting that Job himself will see God. Verses 28-29 turn back to warn the friends that judgment awaits them too. The contrast is deliberate: the more completely Job is abandoned by everyone, the more fiercely he holds to the one who will stand for him.

outline.t: God, not Job, has done this
Abandoned by all: have pity on me
My Redeemer lives, and I will see God

doctrines.note: Verses 25-27 are one of the Old Testament's strongest expressions of hope beyond present suffering. Job expects to be vindicated and to see God himself, even after his skin has been destroyed.

The Redeemer is the one who acts for a helpless relative, buying back, rescuing, and vindicating. Job's confidence that such a Redeemer lives is a confession that rescue will come from outside himself.

The chapter shows suffering as isolation: loss of family, friends, servants, and respect. Scripture treats that loneliness as a real part of affliction, and Job's hope rises from inside it, not after it.

words.note: Ga'al, to redeem, act as kinsman, buy back. Its participle go'el names the next of kin who rescues, redeems, or avenges a family member. In verse 25 Job calls someone my Redeemer, the one who will take up his cause. The same word is used of God redeeming Israel.

Acharon, last or latter. In verse 25 it is rendered in the end: the Redeemer will stand upon the earth at the last. It can mean last in time, or be a title, the last one, the one who has the final word, as a witness who stands up last in court.

Chay, living or alive. Job's Redeemer lives (verse 25), in contrast to Job, who is wasting away, and to his dead children. The same word appears in the frequent oath formula as the LORD lives, and in the title the living God.

Sepher, a written document, scroll, or book. In verse 23 Job wishes his words were inscribed in a book, and then, not content even with that, carved into rock. His wish for a lasting record is ironically fulfilled in the book of Job itself.

christ: Job's Redeemer is not named, and the Christian reading of this passage should be held with care. In the Old Testament, God is repeatedly called Israel's Redeemer, and many interpreters think Job means God himself, who will finally stand up for him. The New Testament does not quote this verse, but Christians have long read it in light of Christ, because the church confesses that God has acted as Redeemer in the person of Jesus. He is the true next of kin, sharing our flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14), who pays the price of redemption (Ephesians 1:7; 1 Peter 1:18-19). His resurrection is the first instance of what Job hopes for: a living Redeemer standing on the earth, and the promise that those who belong to him will see God in the flesh (1 Corinthians 15:20-23; 1 John 3:2). Handel set verse 25 at the opening of the third part of Messiah, and the verse is often read at Christian funerals for this reason.

hard.q: Who is Job's Redeemer, and does he expect to see God after death?
hard.a: Both questions are debated. On the Redeemer's identity, many scholars think Job means God himself, appealing from God as accuser to God as vindicator, as in 16:19. Others think Job imagines a heavenly figure distinct from God who will defend him, like the witness or advocate of chapter 16. Christians have read the verse in light of Christ, who is both God and the kinsman of humanity, while recognizing that Job himself could not have known of Jesus. On the second question, the Hebrew of verses 26-27 is difficult. The phrase rendered in my flesh can also be translated apart from my flesh, and the timing of even after my skin has been destroyed is unclear. Some read these verses as hope of bodily resurrection; others as hope of vindication after death but without resurrection; others as hope of seeing God before death, in this life, despite Job's wasting body (which is in fact what happens in chapter 42). What is not in doubt is Job's certainty that he will see God for himself, and not as a stranger.

questions: Job loses brothers, friends, servants, and the respect of his family. Who has stood by you in hard times, and for whom could you be that person?
The go'el was the relative who stepped in when someone could not help himself. What does it mean to you that the Bible describes God, and Christians describe Christ, as that kind of Redeemer?
Job says he will see God for himself, and not as a stranger. What would it mean for you to know God personally rather than only knowing about him?
